messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Hairdresser
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 37

Samir is thirty-eight years old, and he has been cutting hair in the same small salon in the East Village for fourteen years. He is a thin man, with quick, precise hands and a habit of holding his breath when he concentrates. When he speaks about his work, which he does with a kind of weary fondness, he describes the ritual of it—the snip of the shears, the weight of wet hair, the quiet trust of a client leaning back into the sink. For a long time, this was enough. It was a life, he says. A good one.

He does not say this anymore.

The trouble began two years ago, in late October. Samir had been feeling tired for weeks, a bone-deep exhaustion that no amount of sleep could touch. He dismissed it as the autumn grind, the short days and long hours. Then came the fevers, low and persistent, and a cough that rattled in his chest like something trying to get out. He went to a walk-in clinic, then to an urgent care, then to the emergency room. Each time, they sent him home with antibiotics and a shrug. It was only when he collapsed at the salon—mid-snip, a client’s hair half-cut, the scissors clattering to the tile floor—that anyone listened.

The diagnosis was sepsis, stemming from a bacterial infection that had burrowed into the lining of his heart. Endocarditis, they called it. He was in the ICU for eleven days. He remembers the ceiling tiles most clearly. White, perforated, with tiny pinprick holes that seemed to stare back at him. He remembers the hiss of the ventilator, the beep of the monitors, the way the nurses would float in and out of his field of vision like ghosts. He remembers the moment, sometime on the third night, when a doctor sat down beside his bed and said, very quietly, “We’re doing everything we can.”

Samir heard the words. He understood them, in the way you understand a foreign language you once studied. He felt the floor drop out from under him, even though he was already lying flat on his back. He thought, *This is it. This is where I die.*

He did not die. The antibiotics worked. The surgery to repair his mitral valve was successful. He was discharged after a month, weak and thin, with a scar like a zipper down the center of his chest. The physical recovery was slow, but predictable. He went to cardiac rehab. He walked around his apartment. He learned to breathe without flinching.

But something else had taken root. It was not in his heart. It was in the air around him.

Now, two years later, Samir cannot be alone in a room without a window. He cannot fall asleep without the television on, because the silence sounds like the ICU at night. He checks his pulse constantly—on the subway, during a haircut, while standing in line at the bodega. He has three different blood pressure cuffs at home, and he uses them all. He has called 911 four times in the past year for symptoms that turned out to be nothing: a racing heart from caffeine, a stitch in his side from anxiety. Each time, he feels a wave of relief so intense it makes him nauseous, followed by a shame that lingers for days.

At work, he has become a different kind of hairdresser. He used to chat easily, moving from client to client with a natural rhythm. Now he finds himself scanning their faces for signs of illness. A flush of skin, a labored breath, a cough. He has started wearing a mask, even though no one else does. He washes his hands until they crack and bleed. He cut a client’s hair last week—a young woman, a regular—and when she mentioned she had just gotten over a cold, he felt a bolt of pure terror. He finished the cut in silence, his hands shaking. After she left, he sanitized every surface, every comb, every chair. He went home and took a shower so hot it left his skin raw.

He no longer goes to the doctor. Not for anything. Not for a checkup, not for a blood test, not for the lingering pain in his chest that the cardiologist says is just scar tissue. The thought of sitting in that waiting room, of smelling the antiseptic, of hearing a stethoscope touch his skin—it makes him feel like he is drowning. He knows this is irrational. He knows that avoiding the doctor is dangerous. But the alternative, he says, is worse. The alternative is going back to that room, back to those ceiling tiles, back to the moment when a stranger told him he might not wake up.

Samir is single. He has not dated since before the illness. He tells himself it is because he is too busy, too tired, too set in his ways. But the truth is simpler and harder. He cannot imagine letting anyone close enough to see him the way he is now. He cannot imagine someone touching his chest, tracing the line of the scar. He cannot imagine explaining why he wakes up three times a night, drenched in sweat, convinced that his heart has stopped.

He still cuts hair. He is good at it. He stands behind the chair, his shears in hand, and for an hour or two, he almost forgets. But the moment the client leaves, the silence returns. And Samir finds himself checking his pulse again.
